decks.title: Complex Numbers - Part 1: Algebra, conjugate and modulus
goals: Explain why real numbers are not enough and use the imaginary unit i
Add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers and find the additive and multiplicative inverse
Find unknown parts from the equality of two complex numbers
Find the conjugate and the modulus and use their properties

slides.heading: Complex Numbers, Part 1: Algebra, conjugate and modulus
slides.body_md: Some equations have no real solution. What new numbers make them solvable?

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why we need new numbers, powers of i, adding, subtracting and multiplying, inverses and division, and finally the conjugate and the modulus.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part one. The equation x squared plus one equals zero has no real solution, so mathematicians invented a new number whose square is minus one. In this part you meet that number, its powers, and the algebra of complex numbers, and you learn the conjugate and the modulus.

slides.heading: Why we need new numbers
slides.body_md: Each enlargement of the number system solved equations the old one could not. $x^2 = -1$ has no real solution, so we introduce a number $i$ with $i^2 = -1$.

headers: Smallest number system with a solution

visual.alt: Table of four equations and the smallest number system that solves each: x plus 5 equals 2 needs the integers, with x equal minus 3; 3x equals 7 needs the rational numbers; x squared equals 2 needs the real numbers; and x squared equals minus 1 needs the complex numbers, with solutions plus or minus i.
visual.caption: Each enlargement of the numbers solves equations the last one could not.

slides.narration: Look at the four equations. Adding five to x gives two, which needs negative integers. Three x equals seven needs fractions. X squared equals two needs real numbers. Finally x squared equals minus one needs a new kind of number, the imaginary unit, written i, whose square is minus one. The numbers built from it are called complex numbers.

slides.heading: The imaginary unit and the form a + ib
slides.body_md: A complex number is $z = a + ib$ with $a$ and $b$ real: $a$ is the **real part** and $b$ the **imaginary part**. It is real when $b = 0$ and purely imaginary when $a = 0$ and $b \ne 0$.

visual.alt: Table of five complex numbers with their real and imaginary parts: 9 minus 2 i has real part 9 and imaginary part minus 2; minus 4 plus 6 i has parts minus 4 and 6; 11 is real; 7 i is purely imaginary; and one half minus three quarters i has parts one half and minus three quarters.
visual.caption: $z = a + ib$: the imaginary part is the real number $b$, not $ib$.

slides.narration: A complex number has a real part and an imaginary part. Note that the imaginary part is the real number b, without the letter i. If the imaginary part is zero the number is real, and if the real part is zero the number is purely imaginary. Every real number is a complex number, so the complex numbers include all the numbers you already know.

slides.heading: Powers of i
slides.body_md: $i, -1, -i, 1$ repeat in a cycle of four. Divide the exponent by $4$ and keep the remainder; negative exponents follow the same cycle.

visual.alt: Table of powers of i by division of the exponent by 4: i to the 12 is 1, i to the 25 is i, i to the 38 is minus 1, i to the 47 is minus i; negative exponents follow the same cycle, so i to the minus 5 is minus i and i to the minus 10 is minus 1.
visual.caption: Write $n = 4q + r$ with $0 \le r \le 3$; then $i^n = i^r$.

slides.narration: The first four powers of i are i, minus one, minus i and one, and then they repeat. So to find any power, divide the exponent by four and look at the remainder. A remainder of zero gives one, one gives i, two gives minus one and three gives minus i. The same rule works for negative exponents, as the last two rows show.

slides.heading: Quick check: powers in a family
slides.body_md: Decide whether one value serves for a whole family of powers.
slides.narration: Write the exponent as four k plus two and use the cycle of powers.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a sum of powers

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: i to the 74 is minus 1, i to the minus 37 is minus i, and i to the 19 squared is minus 1; the sum is minus 2 minus i.
visual.caption: Reduce each exponent, then add.

slides.narration: Reduce each exponent separately. Seventy four leaves remainder two, so the first power is minus one. Minus thirty seven is four times minus ten plus three, so the second power is minus i. Nineteen leaves remainder three, so i to the nineteen is minus i, and its square is minus one. The sum is minus two minus i.

slides.heading: Sum, difference and additive inverse
slides.body_md: Add or subtract the real parts and the imaginary parts separately. The **additive inverse** of $z$ is $-z$, because $z + (-z) = 0$.

visual.alt: Table for z one equal minus 2 plus 7 i and z two equal 5 minus 3 i: the sum is 3 plus 4 i, the difference is minus 7 plus 10 i, the additive inverse of z one is 2 minus 7 i, and a number plus its additive inverse is 0.
visual.caption: $z_1 = -2 + 7i$, $z_2 = 5 - 3i$: work part by part.

slides.narration: Adding complex numbers is like collecting like terms. Add the real parts together and the imaginary parts together. For subtraction, subtract each part and watch the signs. The additive inverse of a number is the number with both parts changed in sign, and a number plus its additive inverse is zero.

slides.heading: Product
slides.body_md: Multiply like brackets and replace $i^2$ by $-1$: $(a + ib)(c + id) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i$.

visual.alt: Table showing the product of 6 plus i and 2 minus 3 i: expand into four terms, replace i squared by minus 1, and collect to get 15 minus 16 i.
visual.caption: Expand like brackets, then use $i^2 = -1$.

slides.narration: To multiply, expand the brackets as usual. You get four terms. The term with i squared becomes minus one times its coefficient. In the table, six plus i times two minus three i gives twelve, minus eighteen i, plus two i, minus three i squared. The last term becomes plus three, and the answer is fifteen minus sixteen i.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a difference of squares

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table: three plus 2 i squared is 5 plus 12 i, three minus 2 i squared is 5 minus 12 i, and their difference is 24 i, which is purely imaginary.
visual.caption: The real parts cancel and only the imaginary part survives.

slides.narration: Square each bracket. Three plus two i squared is nine plus twelve i plus four i squared, which is five plus twelve i. The second square is five minus twelve i. When we subtract, the real parts cancel and the imaginary parts double, leaving twenty four i. The answer is purely imaginary.

slides.heading: Quick check: a number and its conjugate
slides.body_md: Multiply two numbers that differ only in the sign of the imaginary part.
slides.narration: Expand and replace i squared by minus one.

slides.heading: Multiplicative inverse and division
slides.body_md: The **multiplicative inverse** of $z \ne 0$ is $\dfrac{1}{z} = \dfrac{\bar z}{|z|^2}$. To divide, multiply the top and the bottom by the **conjugate of the divisor**.

visual.alt: Table of three complex numbers with their conjugates, squared moduli and multiplicative inverses: for 7 plus i the squared modulus is 50 and the inverse is 7 over 50 minus 1 over 50 i; for 4 minus 9 i it is 97; for minus 3 minus 2 i it is 13.
visual.caption: The inverse is the conjugate divided by $|z|^2$.

slides.narration: The product of a number and its conjugate is real, and equals the sum of the squares of its parts. So the inverse of a number is its conjugate divided by that sum. The table shows three examples. To divide by a complex number, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the divisor, which makes the denominator real.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a quotient
slides.body_md: Express $\dfrac{14 - 5i}{4 + i}$ in the form $a + ib$.

visual.alt: Table dividing 14 minus 5 i by 4 plus i: multiply top and bottom by 4 minus i, the numerator is 51 minus 34 i, the denominator is 17, the quotient is 3 minus 2 i and multiplying back gives 14 minus 5 i.
visual.caption: Division is rationalising with the conjugate.

slides.narration: Multiply top and bottom by four minus i. The numerator expands to fifty six, minus fourteen i, minus twenty i, plus five i squared, which is fifty one minus thirty four i. The denominator is sixteen plus one, which is seventeen. Dividing each part by seventeen gives three minus two i. Check by multiplying three minus two i by four plus i.

slides.heading: Quick check: a quotient with a real numerator
slides.body_md: Divide a real number by a complex number.
slides.narration: Multiply top and bottom by five plus i.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: equal complex numbers
slides.body_md: Find real $x$ and $y$ if $(3x - y) + i(2x + 5y) = 11 + 13i$.

visual.alt: Table solving the equation 3x minus y plus i times 2x plus 5y equal 11 plus 13 i: equate the real parts and the imaginary parts, eliminate y to get 17x equal 68, so x is 4 and y is 1, and check.
visual.caption: $a + ib = c + id \iff a = c$ and $b = d$.

slides.narration: Two complex numbers are equal when their real parts are equal and their imaginary parts are equal. So one complex equation gives two real equations. Three x minus y equals eleven, and two x plus five y equals thirteen. Multiply the first by five and add to get seventeen x equals sixty eight, so x is four and y is one.

slides.heading: The conjugate and its rules
slides.body_md: The **conjugate** of $z = a + ib$ is $\bar z = a - ib$. It passes through sums, products and quotients, and $z + \bar z = 2a$, $z - \bar z = 2ib$, $z\bar z = a^2 + b^2$.

visual.alt: Table checking the conjugate rules for z one equal 2 plus 7 i and z two equal 4 minus 3 i: the conjugate of the sum 6 plus 4 i is 6 minus 4 i on both sides; the conjugate of the product 29 plus 22 i is 29 minus 22 i on both sides; and the conjugate of the quotient is minus 13 over 25 minus 34 over 25 i on both sides.
visual.caption: $z_1 = 2 + 7i$, $z_2 = 4 - 3i$: the conjugate passes through sums, products and quotients.

math: \bar z = a - ib,\quad z\bar z = a^2 + b^2
slides.narration: The conjugate keeps the real part and changes the sign of the imaginary part. The conjugate of a sum is the sum of the conjugates, and the same holds for products and quotients. The table checks each rule for the numbers two plus seven i and four minus three i. A number is real exactly when it equals its own conjugate.

slides.heading: The modulus and its rules
slides.body_md: $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ is the distance of $z$ from the origin. $|z_1z_2| = |z_1||z_2|$, $\left|\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right| = \dfrac{|z_1|}{|z_2|}$, $|\bar z| = |z|$ and $z\bar z = |z|^2$.

visual.alt: Table checking four modulus rules for z one equal 1 plus 4 i and z two equal 5 minus 2 i: the product 13 plus 18 i has modulus root 493, which is root 17 times root 29; the quotient has modulus about 0.766 both ways; a number and its conjugate have modulus root 17; and z times its conjugate is 17, the modulus squared.
visual.caption: $z_1 = 1 + 4i$, $z_2 = 5 - 2i$.

slides.narration: The modulus is the size of a complex number, found with the Pythagorean theorem. The modulus of a product is the product of the moduli, and the modulus of a quotient is the quotient of the moduli. A number and its conjugate have the same modulus, and a number times its conjugate equals the modulus squared. The table checks all four rules.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: modulus without expanding
slides.body_md: Find $\left|\dfrac{(1 + 4i)^2}{5 - 2i}\right|$.

visual.alt: Table finding the modulus of 1 plus 4 i squared over 5 minus 2 i: the square is minus 15 plus 8 i with modulus 17, the denominator has modulus root 29, so the answer is 17 over root 29, and direct division gives minus 91 plus 10 i over 29 whose modulus is 17 root 29 over 29.
visual.caption: Use the rules for the modulus before expanding anything.

slides.narration: Use the rules before expanding anything. The modulus of one plus four i is root seventeen, so the modulus of its square is seventeen. The modulus of five minus two i is root twenty nine. The quotient is seventeen over root twenty nine, which is seventeen root twenty nine over twenty nine. The table confirms it by dividing out.

slides.heading: Quick check: a conjugate
slides.body_md: Write down a conjugate.
slides.narration: Change the sign of the imaginary part only.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $i^2 = -1$; powers of $i$ repeat in a cycle of four
Add and subtract part by part; multiply like brackets
$\dfrac{1}{z} = \dfrac{\bar z}{|z|^2}$; divide with the conjugate of the divisor

nodes.label: Inverse $\dfrac{\bar z}{|z|^2}$; divide with the conjugate

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: the imaginary unit squares to minus 1 and its powers repeat; complex numbers add, subtract and multiply like brackets; the inverse and division use the conjugate over the squared modulus; and the conjugate and modulus follow simple rules.
visual.caption: Part 1 in four steps.

slides.narration: To sum up. The imaginary unit squares to minus one and its powers cycle with period four. Complex numbers add, subtract and multiply like brackets. The inverse and the quotient use the conjugate, because a number times its conjugate is real. The conjugate and modulus follow simple rules for products and quotients.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Show the **conjugate step** in every quotient
Check a quotient by multiplying back

rows: equating real and imaginary parts 1, two equations solved 2

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: powers of i earn the reduced exponents and the value; a quotient in the form a plus i b earns the conjugate step, the expansion and the answer; finding x and y earns equating the parts and solving; modulus and conjugate rules earn the rule and both sides computed.
visual.caption: Show the conjugate step; it carries the method marks.

slides.narration: In the examination, show the conjugate step in every quotient, since it carries the method mark. Remember that one complex equation gives two real equations, one for each part. Use the rules for the modulus before you expand anything. And check a quotient by multiplying the answer by the divisor.

decks.title: Complex Numbers - Part 2: Argand plane, argument, polar form and roots
goals: Plot complex numbers on the Argand plane and interpret the conjugate and the sum geometrically
Find the principal argument and use the rules for the argument of a product and a quotient
Convert between the form a + ib and the polar form
Find the square roots of a complex number
Use the cube roots of unity and their properties

slides.heading: Complex Numbers, Part 2: Argand plane, polar form and roots
slides.body_md: Every complex number is a point of a plane. What do its distance and direction tell us?

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the Argand plane, the argument and its rules, polar form, square roots of a complex number, and the cube roots of unity.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. A complex number a plus i b can be drawn as the point a comma b. In this part you will read distance and direction from the picture, write numbers in polar form, find square roots of complex numbers, and meet the three cube roots of unity.

slides.heading: The Argand plane
slides.body_md: $a + ib$ is the point $(a, b)$: **real axis** across, **imaginary axis** up. The signs of the two parts give the quadrant.

series.label: arrow from the origin to the point 1
arrow from the origin to the point 2
arrow from the origin to the point 3
arrow from the origin to the point 4

visual.alt: The Argand plane with four points, one in each quadrant: 5 plus 2 i in the first, minus 4 plus 3 i in the second, minus 2 minus 5 i in the third and 3 minus 4 i in the fourth, each joined to the origin. The real part is read along the horizontal axis and the imaginary part along the vertical axis.
visual.caption: $a + ib$ is the point $(a, b)$: real part across, imaginary part up.

slides.narration: In the Argand plane the horizontal axis holds the real part and the vertical axis holds the imaginary part. Five plus two i is five across and two up, in the first quadrant. Minus four plus three i is in the second quadrant, minus two minus five i in the third, and three minus four i in the fourth. Real numbers lie on the horizontal axis.

slides.heading: Conjugate and negative as reflections
slides.body_md: $\bar z$ is the mirror image of $z$ in the **real axis**; $-z$ is its image in the **origin**. All four points $z$, $\bar z$, $-z$, $-\bar z$ are at the same distance from $O$.

series.label: right side of the rectangle
bottom side of the rectangle
left side of the rectangle
top side of the rectangle

visual.alt: The Argand plane with z equal 5 plus 2 i, its conjugate 5 minus 2 i, minus z equal minus 5 minus 2 i and minus the conjugate, minus 5 plus 2 i. The four points are the corners of a rectangle centred at the origin; the conjugate is the mirror image in the real axis and minus z is the image in the origin.
visual.caption: $\bar z$ reflects in the real axis; $-z$ reflects in the origin.

slides.narration: The conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part, so it is the mirror image in the real axis. Minus z flips both parts, so it is the image through the origin. The four numbers five plus two i, five minus two i, minus five minus two i and minus five plus two i are the corners of a rectangle centred at the origin, all at the same distance from it.

slides.heading: Sum as a parallelogram; distance between points
slides.body_md: $z_1 + z_2$ is the fourth corner of the parallelogram on $O$, $z_1$, $z_2$, so $|z_1 + z_2| \le |z_1| + |z_2|$. The distance between the points $z_1$ and $z_2$ is $|z_1 - z_2|$.

series.label: arrow from the origin to z one
arrow from the origin to z two
arrow from the origin to the sum
side parallel to z two
side parallel to z one
segment joining z one and z two

visual.alt: The Argand plane with z one equal minus 2 plus 3 i, z two equal 5 plus i and their sum 3 plus 4 i, the fourth corner of a parallelogram on the origin, z one and z two. The sum has modulus 5, which is less than root 13 plus root 26, about 8.7, and the segment joining z one to z two has length root 53.
visual.caption: $|z_1 + z_2| = 5 < \sqrt{13} + \sqrt{26}$; the distance between the points is $|z_1 - z_2| = \sqrt{53}$.

slides.narration: To add complex numbers on the plane, complete the parallelogram. Minus two plus three i and five plus i have the sum three plus four i, the fourth corner. The diagonal from the origin has length five, shorter than the two sides together, which is the triangle inequality. The distance between two points is the modulus of their difference.

slides.heading: The argument by position
slides.body_md: The **principal argument** $\theta$ lies in $(-180^\circ, 180^\circ]$, measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis. Find the related angle $\alpha$ with $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{|b|}{|a|}$, then place it using the quadrant.

visual.alt: Table of principal arguments: 3 plus 4 i has 53.13 degrees, minus 3 plus 4 i has 126.87 degrees, minus 3 minus 4 i has minus 126.87 degrees and 3 minus 4 i has minus 53.13 degrees, all from the related angle 53.13 degrees; the positive real axis has 0, the positive imaginary axis 90, the negative real axis 180 and the negative imaginary axis minus 90 degrees.
visual.caption: $\theta = \alpha,\ 180^\circ - \alpha,\ -(180^\circ - \alpha),\ -\alpha$ in quadrants I, II, III, IV.

slides.narration: The principal argument is the angle from the positive real axis to the line from the origin to the point, between minus one hundred eighty and one hundred eighty degrees. Find the related acute angle from the tangent of the absolute values. Then adjust for the quadrant. Points on the axes have the arguments zero, ninety, one hundred eighty and minus ninety degrees.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: two arguments
slides.body_md: Find the modulus and the principal argument of $-12 - 5i$ and of $-15 + 8i$.
bullets: Modulus from the sum of squares: $13$ and $17$

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: minus 12 minus 5 i has modulus 13, lies in quadrant III with related angle 22.62 degrees, so its principal argument is minus 157.38 degrees; minus 15 plus 8 i has modulus 17, lies in quadrant II with related angle 28.07 degrees, so its principal argument is 151.93 degrees.
visual.caption: Find the quadrant first, then place the related angle.

slides.narration: For minus twelve minus five i the modulus is thirteen. It is in the third quadrant with related angle about twenty two point six degrees, so the argument is minus one hundred fifty seven point four degrees. For minus fifteen plus eight i the modulus is seventeen. It is in the second quadrant with related angle about twenty eight degrees, so the argument is one hundred fifty two degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: an axis point
slides.body_md: Give the principal argument of a point on the negative real axis.
slides.narration: Remember which end of the interval is included.

slides.heading: Rules for the argument
slides.body_md: Arguments **add** under multiplication and **subtract** under division, always reduced into $(-180^\circ, 180^\circ]$. Also $\arg\bar z = -\arg z$.

visual.alt: Table checking the argument rules for z one equal 1 plus 2 i and z two equal 3 plus i: the product is 1 plus 7 i with argument 81.87 degrees, equal to 63.43 plus 18.43; the quotient is one half plus one half i with argument 45 degrees, equal to 63.43 minus 18.43; and the conjugate of z one has argument minus 63.43 degrees, the negative of the argument of z one.
visual.caption: $z_1 = 1 + 2i$, $z_2 = 3 + i$: arguments add under products and subtract under quotients (mod $360^\circ$).

slides.narration: The argument turns products into sums. The argument of a product is the sum of the arguments, and the argument of a quotient is their difference. The argument of the conjugate is the negative of the argument. If the result falls outside the principal range, add or subtract three hundred sixty degrees. The table checks all three rules.

slides.heading: Quick check: the argument interval
slides.body_md: Decide whether an end of the principal interval is allowed.
slides.narration: The interval is open at one end and closed at the other.

slides.heading: Polar form
slides.body_md: $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$ with $r = |z|$ and $\theta = \arg z$. Going back, $a = r\cos\theta$ and $b = r\sin\theta$.

visual.alt: Axes with the point z equal 3 root 3 plus 3 i in the first quadrant. The segment from the origin to z has length 6 and makes an angle of 30 degrees with the positive real axis; a dashed perpendicular goes down to the real axis.
visual.caption: $z = 3\sqrt{3} + 3i$: modulus $6$, argument $30^\circ$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: A point can be described by its distance from the origin and its direction. The distance is the modulus r and the direction is the argument theta. For three root three plus three i the modulus is six and the angle is thirty degrees. The polar form is r times cosine theta plus i sine theta. To go back, r cosine theta is the real part and r sine theta is the imaginary part.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: to polar form
slides.body_md: Write $-4\sqrt{3} - 4i$ in polar form.

visual.alt: Table converting minus 4 root 3 minus 4 i to polar form: modulus 8, quadrant III, related angle 30 degrees, principal argument minus 150 degrees, so 8 times cosine of minus 150 degrees plus i sine of minus 150 degrees; expanding gives minus 4 root 3 and minus 4 again.
visual.caption: $z = -4\sqrt{3} - 4i$.

slides.narration: First the modulus: the square root of forty eight plus sixteen is eight. Both parts are negative, so the point is in the third quadrant. The tangent of the related angle is one over root three, so it is thirty degrees. The principal argument is minus one hundred eighty plus thirty, which is minus one hundred fifty degrees. Expanding the polar form returns the original number.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: from polar form
slides.body_md: Write $8(\cos 120^\circ + i\sin 120^\circ)$ and $10(\cos 270^\circ + i\sin 270^\circ)$ in the form $a + ib$.

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: 8 times cosine 120 degrees plus i sine 120 degrees is minus 4 plus 4 root 3 i, and 10 times cosine 270 degrees plus i sine 270 degrees is minus 10 i.
visual.caption: $a = r\cos\theta$ and $b = r\sin\theta$.

slides.narration: Evaluate the cosine and the sine, then multiply by the modulus. At one hundred twenty degrees the cosine is minus one half and the sine is root three over two, so eight times each gives minus four plus four root three i. At two hundred seventy degrees the cosine is zero and the sine is minus one, giving minus ten i.

slides.heading: Products and quotients in polar form
slides.body_md: Multiply the moduli and add the arguments; for a quotient, divide the moduli and subtract the arguments. Multiplying by a number of modulus $1$ turns a point about $O$ without changing its distance.

rows: multiplying the two numbers out gives $0 + 6i$

visual.alt: Table for z one equal 2 times cosine 20 degrees plus i sine 20 degrees and z two equal 3 times cosine 70 degrees plus i sine 70 degrees: the product has modulus 6 and argument 90 degrees, so it is 6 i; the quotient has modulus two thirds and argument minus 50 degrees.
visual.caption: Multiply the moduli and add the arguments.

slides.narration: In polar form, products are easy. Multiply the moduli and add the arguments. For two times cosine twenty degrees plus i sine twenty degrees and three times cosine seventy degrees plus i sine seventy degrees, the modulus is six and the angle is ninety degrees, so the product is six i. For a quotient divide the moduli and subtract the angles.

slides.heading: Square root of a complex number
slides.body_md: Let $(x + iy)^2 = a + ib$. Equate parts, use $x^2 + y^2 = |z|$, solve for $x^2$ and $y^2$, and pair the signs using the sign of $b$.

nodes.label: Equate parts: $x^2 - y^2 = a$ and $2xy = b$
Take roots; the sign of $b$ pairs the signs

visual.alt: Flow diagram of the method for square roots: let x plus i y squared equal a plus i b, equate the real and imaginary parts, add the equation x squared plus y squared equal the modulus, solve for x squared and y squared, take roots and pair the signs by the sign of b, then check by squaring.
visual.caption: Six steps from the equation to the roots.

math: x^2 - y^2 = a,\quad 2xy = b,\quad x^2 + y^2 = |z|
slides.narration: To find a square root, suppose x plus i y squared equals a plus i b. Equating real and imaginary parts gives x squared minus y squared equals a, and two x y equals b. The modulus of the square equals x squared plus y squared. Adding and subtracting gives x squared and y squared. If b is positive the signs match, if negative they are opposite. Always check by squaring.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a square root
slides.body_md: Find the square roots of $-21 - 20i$.

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table: the number minus 21 minus 20 i has modulus 29; x squared is 4 and y squared is 25; the product 2xy is negative so the signs are opposite; the square roots are plus or minus 2 minus 5 i, and squaring 2 minus 5 i gives minus 21 minus 20 i.
visual.caption: Square roots of $z = -21 - 20i$.

slides.narration: The modulus is the square root of four hundred forty one plus four hundred, which is twenty nine. Then x squared is twenty nine minus twenty one over two, which is four, and y squared is twenty five. Since two x y is negative, the signs are opposite. The roots are plus or minus two minus five i. Squaring two minus five i gives minus twenty one minus twenty i.

slides.heading: Quick check: a square root with a letter
slides.body_md: Find the missing part of a square root.
slides.narration: Square the bracket and compare real parts.

slides.heading: The two square roots on the plane
slides.body_md: The roots of $z$ are opposite points. Each has modulus $\sqrt{|z|}$ and half the argument of $z$.

series.label: arrow from the origin to z
arrow from the origin to the first root
arrow from the origin to the second root

visual.alt: The Argand plane with z equal 7 plus 24 i, modulus 25 and argument about 73.74 degrees, and its two square roots 4 plus 3 i and minus 4 minus 3 i. The roots lie at opposite points, each at distance 5, the square root of 25, and the first root has half the argument of z, about 36.87 degrees.
visual.caption: The two roots are opposite points; each has modulus $\sqrt{|z|}$ and half the argument.

slides.narration: Here z equals seven plus twenty four i, with modulus twenty five and argument about seventy four degrees. Its square roots are four plus three i and minus four minus three i. They are opposite points, each at distance five, which is the square root of twenty five. The first root has argument about thirty seven degrees, half that of z.

slides.heading: Cube roots of unity
slides.body_md: $x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1) = 0$ gives $x = 1$ or $x = \dfrac{-1 \pm i\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Write $\omega = \dfrac{-1 + i\sqrt{3}}{2}$; then $\omega^2 = \dfrac{-1 - i\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

visual.alt: Table of the three cube roots of unity: 1, omega equal minus one half plus root 3 over 2 times i, and omega squared equal minus one half minus root 3 over 2 times i. Each has modulus 1, the arguments are 0, 120 and minus 120 degrees, and the cube of each is 1.
visual.caption: $x^3 = 1$ has the roots $1$, $\omega$, $\omega^2$ with $\omega = \dfrac{-1 + i\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

slides.narration: Factorise x cubed minus one into x minus one times x squared plus x plus one. The quadratic factor has two complex roots, minus one plus or minus i root three over two. Call the first one omega. Squaring omega gives the second root. Each of the three numbers has modulus one and cubes to one. Their arguments are zero, one hundred twenty and minus one hundred twenty degrees.

slides.heading: The roots form an equilateral triangle

slides.narration: Two facts do most of the work. The three roots add up to zero, and omega cubed is one. notes.title: Complex Numbers - chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Need for complex numbers and powers of i
sections.body_md:
The equation $x^2 = -1$ has no real solution because $x^2 \ge 0$. We introduce the **imaginary unit** $i$ with $i^2 = -1$. A **complex number** is $z = a + ib$ with $a, b$ real: $a$ is the real part and $b$ (a real number, not $ib$) is the imaginary part.

The powers of $i$ repeat in a cycle of four: $i, -1, -i, 1$. Write $n = 4q + r$ with $0 \le r \le 3$; then $i^n = i^r$, also for negative $n$. Four consecutive powers add to $0$. There is **no ordering** of complex numbers: $2 + i > 1 + i$ has no meaning.

key_terms.definition_md: A number $a + ib$ with $a$ and $b$ real.

headers: Smallest number system with a solution

sections.heading: 2. Algebra of complex numbers
sections.body_md:
**Equality:** $a + ib = c + id$ exactly when $a = c$ and $b = d$; one complex equation gives two real equations.

**Sum and difference:** $(a + ib) \pm (c + id) = (a \pm c) + (b \pm d)i$. The additive inverse of $z$ is $-z$.

**Product:** expand and replace $i^2$ by $-1$: $(a + ib)(c + id) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i$.

**Multiplicative inverse and quotient:** $\dfrac{1}{z} = \dfrac{\bar z}{|z|^2}$. To divide, multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the divisor. Check a quotient by multiplying back.

sections.heading: 3. The conjugate
sections.body_md:
The **conjugate** of $z = a + ib$ is $\bar z = a - ib$.

- $z + \bar z = 2a$ (real) and $z - \bar z = 2ib$ (purely imaginary or zero).
- $z\bar z = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2$.
- $\overline{z_1 \pm z_2} = \bar z_1 \pm \bar z_2$, $\overline{z_1z_2} = \bar z_1\bar z_2$, $\overline{\left(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right)} = \dfrac{\bar z_1}{\bar z_2}$ and $\bar{\bar z} = z$.
- $z$ is real exactly when $\bar z = z$.

key_terms.definition_md: $\bar z = a - ib$, the mirror image of $z$ in the real axis.

visual.alt: Table checking the conjugate rules for z one equal 2 plus 7 i and z two equal 4 minus 3 i: the conjugate of the sum 6 plus 4 i is 6 minus 4 i on both sides; the conjugate of the product 29 plus 22 i is 29 minus 22 i on both sides; and the conjugate of the quotient is minus 13 over 25 minus 34 over 25 i on both sides.

sections.heading: 4. The modulus
sections.body_md:
The **modulus** of $z = a + ib$ is $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, the distance from the origin; keep exact surds.

- $|z| \ge 0$, and $|z| = 0$ only for $z = 0$.
- $|z_1z_2| = |z_1||z_2|$ and $\left|\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right| = \dfrac{|z_1|}{|z_2|}$.
- $|\bar z| = |z| = |-z|$ and $z\bar z = |z|^2$.
- $|z_1 + z_2| \le |z_1| + |z_2|$ (triangle inequality); $|z_1 - z_2|$ is the distance between the points $z_1$ and $z_2$.
- $|z| = k$ is a circle about the origin; $|z - 1| = |z - 5i|$ is a straight line, the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining $1$ and $5i$.

Use the rules to find a modulus **before** expanding.

sections.heading: 5. The Argand plane and the argument
sections.body_md:
The number $a + ib$ is the point $(a, b)$: the **real axis** is horizontal and the **imaginary axis** vertical. The conjugate is the mirror image in the real axis, $-z$ the image in the origin, and $z_1 + z_2$ the fourth corner of the parallelogram on $O, z_1, z_2$.

The **principal argument** $\theta$ lies in $(-180^\circ, 180^\circ]$ and is measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis. With related angle $\alpha$, $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{|b|}{|a|}$: $\theta = \alpha,\ 180^\circ - \alpha,\ -(180^\circ - \alpha),\ -\alpha$ in quadrants I, II, III, IV. The axes give $0^\circ, 90^\circ, 180^\circ, -90^\circ$.

Rules (mod $360^\circ$): $\arg(z_1z_2) = \arg z_1 + \arg z_2$, $\arg\dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \arg z_1 - \arg z_2$, $\arg\bar z = -\arg z$.

sections.heading: 6. Polar form
sections.body_md:
Write $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$ with $r = |z|$ and $\theta = \arg z$. To convert, find $r$, the quadrant, the related angle and then $\theta$; to go back, $a = r\cos\theta$ and $b = r\sin\theta$. Check a polar form by expanding it.

Products and quotients: multiply (divide) the moduli and add (subtract) the arguments, reducing the result into $(-180^\circ, 180^\circ]$. Multiplying by a number of modulus $1$ turns the point about the origin.

sections.heading: 7. Square root of a complex number
sections.body_md:
To find $\sqrt{a + ib}$ let $(x + iy)^2 = a + ib$. Then $x^2 - y^2 = a$ and $2xy = b$, and $x^2 + y^2 = |z|$. Hence $x^2 = \dfrac{|z| + a}{2}$ and $y^2 = \dfrac{|z| - a}{2}$. If $b > 0$ then $x$ and $y$ have the same sign; if $b < 0$ opposite signs; if $b = 0$ and $a < 0$ the roots are $\pm i\sqrt{-a}$.

There are always two roots, $w$ and $-w$, at opposite points of the plane; each has modulus $\sqrt{|z|}$ and half the argument of $z$. Check by squaring.

key_terms.definition_md: A number $w$ with $w^2 = z$; every non-zero $z$ has exactly two.

sections.heading: 8. Cube roots of unity
sections.body_md:
The solutions of $x^3 = 1$ come from $(x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1) = 0$: $1$, $\omega = \dfrac{-1 + i\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\omega^2 = \dfrac{-1 - i\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

Properties: $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0$; $\omega^3 = 1$; $\bar\omega = \omega^2 = \dfrac{1}{\omega}$; $1 + \omega = -\omega^2$ and $1 + \omega^2 = -\omega$; $\omega^n$ depends only on the remainder of $n$ on division by $3$. Each root has modulus $1$, with arguments $0^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $-120^\circ$; they are the corners of an equilateral triangle on the unit circle.

Useful results: $(a + b\omega + c\omega^2)(a + b\omega^2 + c\omega) = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - ab - bc - ca$ and $x^3 + y^3 = (x + y)(x + y\omega)(x + y\omega^2)$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are usually awarded**
- *Quotient in the form $a + ib$ (2-3 marks):* conjugate of the divisor, expansion, answer.
- *Find $x$ and $y$ (3 marks):* equate real and imaginary parts, solve the two equations.
- *Modulus and argument (2-3 marks):* modulus, quadrant and related angle, argument in the principal range.
- *Polar form (3 marks):* modulus, argument, form written.
- *Square root (3 marks):* the equations, $x^2$ and $y^2$, the signed roots.
- *Cube roots of unity (2-3 marks):* reduce the powers, use $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0$, state the value.
- *Section D (5 marks):* parts such as 2 + 3; label each part and show a mark's worth of working per step.

**Common mistakes**
1. Forgetting that $i^2 = -1$ when multiplying.
2. Writing the imaginary part as $ib$ instead of $b$.
3. Dividing without the conjugate of the divisor.
4. $|a + ib| = a + b$ instead of $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
5. Giving the related angle as the argument, or an argument outside $(-180^\circ, 180^\circ]$.
6. Pairing the signs of a square root wrongly: the sign of $2xy$ is the sign of $b$.
7. Using $\omega^n$ without reducing $n$ modulo $3$.
8. Treating $2 + i > 1 + i$ as meaningful: complex numbers are not ordered.

cards.front_md: Why do we need complex numbers?
cards.back_md: Equations such as $x^2 = -1$ have no real root; the number $i$ with $i^2 = -1$ supplies one.

cards.front_md: Form of a complex number and its parts?
cards.back_md: $z = a + ib$; real part $a$, imaginary part $b$ (a real number, not $ib$).

cards.front_md: When is $a + ib$ real? purely imaginary?
cards.back_md: Real when $b = 0$; purely imaginary when $a = 0$ and $b \ne 0$.
$i, -1, -i, 1$ for remainders $1, 2, 3, 0$ of $n$ on division by $4$ (also for negative $n$).

cards.front_md: Sum of four consecutive powers of $i$?
When are $a + ib$ and $c + id$ equal?
cards.back_md: When $a = c$ **and** $b = d$.
$-a - ib$, because $z + (-z) = 0$.
$(ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i$.
$\dfrac{1}{z} = \dfrac{\bar z}{|z|^2} = \dfrac{a - ib}{a^2 + b^2}$.

cards.front_md: How do you divide complex numbers?
cards.back_md: Multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the divisor.
No: $z_1 > z_2$ has no meaning for non-real numbers; only moduli can be compared.
$\bar z = a - ib$, the mirror image of $z$ in the real axis.
$2a$ (real), $2ib$ (purely imaginary or zero) and $a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2$.

cards.front_md: Conjugate of a sum, product and quotient?
cards.back_md: The sum, product and quotient of the conjugates.
$|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, the distance from the origin.
$|z_1 + z_2| \le |z_1| + |z_2|$, with equality only when the numbers point the same way.
The distance between the points $z_1$ and $z_2$.

cards.front_md: Point representing $a + ib$ on the Argand plane?
cards.back_md: $(a, b)$: real part across, imaginary part up.
$(-180^\circ, 180^\circ]$; the negative real axis is $180^\circ$, not $-180^\circ$.

cards.front_md: Argument in quadrants I, II, III, IV from the related angle $\alpha$?
cards.back_md: $\alpha$, $180^\circ - \alpha$, $-(180^\circ - \alpha)$, $-\alpha$.
$\arg z_1 + \arg z_2$, $\arg z_1 - \arg z_2$ and $-\arg z$ (mod $360^\circ$).
$z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$ with $r = |z|$ and $\theta = \arg z$.

questions.stem_md: Find the real numbers $x$ and $y$ for which $\dfrac{x}{1 + i} + \dfrac{y}{2 - i} = 4 - i$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{x}{1 + i} = \dfrac{x(1 - i)}{2}$ and $\dfrac{y}{2 - i} = \dfrac{y(2 + i)}{5}$. The equation becomes $\left(\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{2y}{5}\right) + \left(-\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{y}{5}\right)i = 4 - i$.

Equating parts: $\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{2y}{5} = 4$ and $-\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{y}{5} = -1$. Adding gives $\dfrac{3y}{5} = 3$, so $y = 5$; then $\dfrac{x}{2} = 4 - 2 = 2$, so $x = 4$.

questions.stem_md: Let $\omega$ be a non-real cube root of $1$. Evaluate the product $(1 - \omega)(1 - \omega^2)(1 - \omega^4)(1 - \omega^5)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Since $\omega^3 = 1$, $\omega^4 = \omega$ and $\omega^5 = \omega^2$. The product is $[(1 - \omega)(1 - \omega^2)]^2$.

Now $(1 - \omega)(1 - \omega^2) = 1 - \omega - \omega^2 + \omega^3 = 1 - (\omega + \omega^2) + 1 = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3$. So the value is $3^2 = 9$.

Using $\omega + \omega^2 = -1$ and $\omega^3 = 1$, this is $x^2 - xy + y^2$. Then $(x + y)(x^2 - xy + y^2) = x^3 + y^3$.

questions.stem_md: The point $z = x + iy$ moves so that $|z - 1| = |z - 5i|$. Find the equation of its path in $x$ and $y$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$|z - 1|^2 = (x - 1)^2 + y^2$ and $|z - 5i|^2 = x^2 + (y - 5)^2$. Setting them equal: $x^2 - 2x + 1 + y^2 = x^2 + y^2 - 10y + 25$.

Simplifying gives $x - 5y + 12 = 0$, a straight line: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the points $1$ and $5i$.

questions.solution_md: Square both moduli and compare.

questions.stem_md:
Let $z = \dfrac{1 + i}{1 - i}$.

(a) Show that $z = i$. [2]

(b) Find the value of $z^{66} + z^{-45}$. [2]

(c) Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $z^n = 1$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Multiply the numerator and the denominator by $1 + i$: $z = \dfrac{(1 + i)^2}{1 + 1} = \dfrac{1 + 2i - 1}{2} = \dfrac{2i}{2} = i$.

(b) Since $z = i$, $z^{66} = i^{66}$ with $66 = 4(16) + 2$, so $i^{66} = -1$. Also $-45 = 4(-12) + 3$, so $z^{-45} = i^3 = -i$. The value is $-1 - i$.

(c) The powers of $i$ are $i, -1, -i, 1$, so $i^n = 1$ first when $n = 4$.

questions.solution_md: Rationalise to get $z = i$; reduce exponents modulo $4$.

questions.stem_md:
Let $z = x + iy$ with $z \ne -1$.

(a) Write $\dfrac{z - 1}{z + 1}$ in the form $u + iv$, giving $u$ and $v$ in terms of $x$ and $y$. [3]

(b) The quotient is purely imaginary and not zero. Show that $|z| = 1$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Multiply the numerator and the denominator by $\bar{(z + 1)} = (x + 1) - iy$. The numerator is $(x - 1 + iy)(x + 1 - iy) = (x^2 - 1 + y^2) + 2yi$, and the denominator is $(x + 1)^2 + y^2$.

So $u = \dfrac{x^2 + y^2 - 1}{(x + 1)^2 + y^2}$ and $v = \dfrac{2y}{(x + 1)^2 + y^2}$.

(b) Purely imaginary means $u = 0$, so $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, that is $|z| = 1$. (Non-zero means $v \ne 0$, so $y \ne 0$.)

questions.solution_md: Rationalise with the conjugate of the denominator; set the real part to zero.

questions.stem_md:
Let $z = -3\sqrt{3} + 3i$ and $w = 1 + i\sqrt{3}$.

(a) Find the modulus and the principal argument of $z$, and write $z$ in polar form. [3]

(b) The modulus of $w$ is $2$ and its argument is $60^\circ$. Use the rules for products to find the modulus and principal argument of $zw$, and write $zw$ in the form $a + ib$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $|z| = \sqrt{27 + 9} = 6$. The related angle has $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{3}{3\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, so $\alpha = 30^\circ$. The point is in quadrant II, so $\arg z = 180^\circ - 30^\circ = 150^\circ$ and $z = 6(\cos 150^\circ + i\sin 150^\circ)$.

(b) Moduli multiply and arguments add: $|zw| = 6 \times 2 = 12$ and $\arg(zw) = 150^\circ + 60^\circ = 210^\circ$, which is $-150^\circ$ in the principal range. So $zw = 12(\cos(-150^\circ) + i\sin(-150^\circ)) = 12\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) + 12\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)i = -6\sqrt{3} - 6i$.

questions.solution_md: Related angle and quadrant for $z$; multiply moduli, add arguments for $zw$.

questions.stem_md:
The numbers $z_1 = 1 + 2i$, $z_2 = 5 + 3i$ and $z_3 = 2 - 2i$ are represented on the Argand plane by the points $A$, $B$ and $C$.

(a) Find the lengths $AB$, $AC$ and $BC$. [2]

(b) Show that triangle $ABC$ is right-angled and isosceles, and find its area. [2]

(c) Show that $z_3 - z_1 = -i(z_2 - z_1)$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $AB = |z_2 - z_1| = |4 + i| = \sqrt{17}$, $AC = |z_3 - z_1| = |1 - 4i| = \sqrt{17}$ and $BC = |z_3 - z_2| = |-3 - 5i| = \sqrt{34}$.

(b) $AB = AC$, so the triangle is isosceles. Also $AB^2 + AC^2 = 17 + 17 = 34 = BC^2$, so the angle at $A$ is a right angle. The area is $\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot AB\cdot AC = \dfrac{17}{2}$.

(c) $-i(z_2 - z_1) = -i(4 + i) = -4i - i^2 = 1 - 4i$, which is $z_3 - z_1$.

questions.solution_md: Distances are moduli of differences; test with the converse of Pythagoras.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Find the square roots of $11 - 60i$. [3]

(b) Hence write down the square roots of $-11 + 60i$, explaining your method. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Let $(x + iy)^2 = 11 - 60i$. Then $x^2 - y^2 = 11$ and $2xy = -60$. The modulus is $|z| = \sqrt{121 + 3600} = 61$, so $x^2 + y^2 = 61$.

Hence $x^2 = \dfrac{61 + 11}{2} = 36$ and $y^2 = \dfrac{61 - 11}{2} = 25$. Since $2xy < 0$, the roots are $\pm(6 - 5i)$.

(b) Since $-11 + 60i = i^2(11 - 60i)$, its square roots are $\pm i(6 - 5i)$. Now $i(6 - 5i) = 6i + 5 = 5 + 6i$, so the roots are $\pm(5 + 6i)$. Check: $(5 + 6i)^2 = 25 + 60i - 36 = -11 + 60i$.

questions.solution_md: Method of equating parts for (a); multiply the roots by $i$ for (b).

questions.stem_md:
Let $\omega$ be a complex cube root of unity, so $\omega^3 = 1$ and $\omega \ne 1$.

(a) Starting from $\omega^3 - 1 = 0$, show that $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0$. [2]

(b) Hence simplify $(3 + 3\omega + 5\omega^2)(3 + 5\omega + 3\omega^2)$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\omega^3 - 1 = (\omega - 1)(\omega^2 + \omega + 1) = 0$. Since $\omega \ne 1$, the factor $\omega - 1$ is not zero, so $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0$.

(b) $3 + 3\omega + 5\omega^2 = 3(1 + \omega + \omega^2) + 2\omega^2 = 2\omega^2$ and $3 + 5\omega + 3\omega^2 = 3(1 + \omega + \omega^2) + 2\omega = 2\omega$.

The product is $2\omega^2\cdot 2\omega = 4\omega^3 = 4$.

questions.solution_md: Factorise $\omega^3 - 1$; group each bracket with $1 + \omega + \omega^2$.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write $\omega = \dfrac{-1 + i\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\omega^2$ in polar form. [2]

(b) The points $1$, $\omega$ and $\omega^2$ are plotted on the Argand plane. Find the three distances between them and deduce the shape of the triangle they form. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $|\omega| = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4}} = 1$. The point $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$ is in quadrant II with related angle $60^\circ$, so $\omega = \cos 120^\circ + i\sin 120^\circ$. Also $\omega^2 = \dfrac{-1 - i\sqrt{3}}{2} = \cos 240^\circ + i\sin 240^\circ$, which has principal argument $-120^\circ$.

(b) $1 - \omega = \dfrac{3 - i\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $|1 - \omega|^2 = \dfrac{9 + 3}{4} = 3$. Next $\omega - \omega^2 = i\sqrt{3}$, so $|\omega - \omega^2| = \sqrt{3}$. Finally $\omega^2 - 1 = \dfrac{-3 - i\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $|\omega^2 - 1|^2 = 3$.

All three distances equal $\sqrt{3}$, so the triangle is equilateral.

questions.solution_md: Modulus and argument of $\omega$; distances are moduli of differences.

questions.stem_md: In the complex number $9 - 4i$, the imaginary part, which is a real number, equals ____.
questions.solution_md: Writing $9 - 4i = 9 + (-4)i$, the imaginary part is the coefficient of $i$, namely $-4$.

questions.stem_md: For $z = -2 + 5i$, the sum $z + \bar z$ equals ____.
questions.solution_md: $z + \bar z = (-2 + 5i) + (-2 - 5i) = -4$, which is twice the real part.

questions.stem_md: The point $6i$ lies on the positive imaginary axis, so its principal argument is ____ degrees.
questions.solution_md: The positive imaginary axis is a quarter turn anticlockwise from the positive real axis, so the principal argument is $90^\circ$.
